## How the guide defines it

## How the guide uses it

On 213 pages. Every team's right-hand page prints two playoff markets — a price to win the CFP Championship and a price to make the playoff — so the concept is on the board for all 138 teams whether or not the prose discusses it. p. 4's grid asks each of 22 contributors for a final four, two title-game teams and a champion; nine of the 62 best bets are playoff bets.

## Working definition — TTW DERIVED

The College Football Playoff, a 12-team postseason field, and the futures markets attached to reaching it or winning it.

## Why it matters — TTW DERIVED

It reorganises what a good season means. The guide's contributors repeatedly argue that a hard schedule is now an asset rather than a liability, because the committee wants to see marquee wins — Zachary Cohen makes that case explicitly for BYU.

## How bettors use it in this guide

As a futures market and as a framing device. Makinen uses it to reason about Group of Five access, expecting one such team in this year rather than the two that got in last season, and names Boise State as the likeliest.

## Where it appears

p. 4 for the contributor grid; pp. 5–15 for the priced bets; every team page for the two printed prices; p. 38 for the market's effect on futures handle.

## Caution

The p. 4 grid asks for a **final four** while the field holds **twelve**. A contributor can consistently project four teams and bet a fifth to make the playoff; reading those as contradictions would manufacture a conflict the guide does not contain.
